problem.text: The smallest three positive proper divisors of an integer $n$ are $d_1 < d_2 < d_3$ so that $d_1 + d_2 + d_3 = 57$. Find the sum of the possible values of $d_2$.

steps.title: Where to start: the smallest divisor is always 1
steps.body: The problem is about the smallest divisors of $n$, and the very smallest positive divisor of any integer is $1$. A proper divisor is any divisor other than $n$ itself, so $1$ counts, and $d_1 = 1$.

steps.title: What can $d_2$ and $d_3$ be?
steps.body: Any divisor of $d_2$ also divides $n$, so if $d_2$ had a factor strictly between $1$ and $d_2$, that factor would be a smaller divisor of $n$. So $d_2$ is prime: call it $p$, the smallest prime factor of $n$. In the same way, the only divisors of $d_3$ between $1$ and $d_3$ can be $p$. So $d_3$ is either another prime $q > p$, or $d_3 = p^2$.

your_turn.prompt: Can $p = 2$? Check what $d_3$ would have to be.
your_turn.answer: No. Then $d_3 = 54$, which is neither prime nor $2^2 = 4$ (and $3$ would divide $n$ and be smaller than $54$).

steps.title: Case 1: $d_3$ is a prime $q$
steps.body: We need primes $p < q$ with $p + q = 56$. Try each odd prime $p$ below $28$ and check whether $56 - p$ is prime. Every pair that works really occurs with $n = pq$: for example $n = 3\cdot 53 = 159$ has proper divisors $1, 3, 53$.

your_turn.answer: $p = 3, 13, 19$ (giving $53, 43, 37$). The others give $51, 49, 45, 39, 33$, which are not prime.

steps.title: Case 2: $d_3 = p^2$
steps.body: Now $p + p^2 = 56$, that is $p(p+1) = 56 = 7\cdot 8$. Since $p(p+1)$ grows as $p$ grows, $p = 7$ is the only solution. This happens for $n = 7^3 = 343$, whose proper divisors are $1, 7, 49$.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: Both cases together give the possible values $d_2 = 3, 13, 19$ (Case 1) and $d_2 = 7$ (Case 2), and there are no others. Careful: do not forget the $p^2$ case. The sum is $3 + 13 + 19 + 7 = 42$. The answer is **$42$**.
